auxiliary_material: Background information on SCFA biological roles (immune regulation, glucose homeostasis). Troubleshooting guide for common GC-MS issues (e.g., vacuum pressure, peak repeatability). Comparison of this alkaline extraction method to previous acidic phase separation methods, noting reduced volatility. General recommendations for minimizing freeze-thaw cycles to preserve sample integrity.
outline_action: Use this study to describe the technical methodology for SCFA quantification in serum within the review. Explicitly note that this protocol covers SCFAs but not inosine. Highlight the lack of TME-specific protocols and cancer-specific reference ranges as a limitation in current standardization. Search for additional literature specifically addressing inosine quantification and TME metabolite sampling.
remaining_gap: This study does not provide a measurement protocol for inosine. It does not address sample preparation or quantification specifically for tumor microenvironment (TME) tissue, focusing only on serum and feces. The reference ranges cited are from a general metabolomics database (HMDB) rather than a cancer-specific consensus statement or standardized reference range for tumor patients. The success criterion regarding 'consensus statements' or 'reference ranges' for cancer contexts remains unmet.
useful_material: This study provides a detailed Basic Protocol 1 for quantifying 14 short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in human serum and feces using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). It specifies alkaline extraction (pH > 7) using sodium hydroxide, derivatization with MTBSTFA at 60 °C, and specific GC-MS parameters (e.g., oven temperature program, ion source settings). It includes a table of 14 SCFA standards with retention times and quantification masses. It references the Human Metabolomics Database (HMDB) for normal concentration ranges of acetic acid in human blood (26.8 to 64.2 μM). It outlines calibration curve requirements (R2 ≥ 0.95) and sample storage conditions (−80 °C for long-term).
